quote: Adding an (opt-in) Cyclone/Rust inspired memory ownership model to Swift is highly desired by systems programmers
note: The Swift Ownership Manifesto (swift/docs/OwnershipManifesto.md) notes 'many similarities between shared values and Rust's concept of an immutable borrow'. Lattner's homepage lists Rust among Swift's sources of ideas. The ownership part is well supported; a general 'safety' influence is not specifically documented.

label: approachability, script-like top level
citation: Lattner, C. (n.d.). Chris Lattner's Homepage. nondot.org.
quote: drawing ideas from Objective-C, Rust, Haskell, Ruby, Python, C#, CLU, and far too many others to list.
audit_note: Version 3: quote and source updated.

label: protocols akin to type classes
citation: Lattner, C., interviewed by Arment, M., Liss, C., & Siracusa, J. (2017). ATP Episode 205: Chris Lattner Interview Transcript. Accidental Tech Podcast.

note: Label revised to match the source. Lattner does not name the construct; reading it as type classes is an inference. No Lattner or Apple source found that ties Optional to Maybe, and the Swift Generics Manifesto does not mention Haskell. Lattner's homepage lists Haskell among Swift's sources of ideas.

label: based on Ada
citation: Oracle (2005). Oracle Database PL/SQL User's Guide and Reference 10g Release 2 (10.2), Appendix C: PL/SQL Program Limits.

note: Label revised to match the source. Oracle states the Ada basis directly but does not list which features came from Ada; block syntax, packages and exceptions are Ada-like, but this source does not say they were inherited.

label: classes & objects
citation: Kay, A. C. (1993). The Early History of Smalltalk. ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3) (HOPL-II).
quote: It is not too much of an exaggeration to say that most of my ideas from then on took their roots from Simula—but not as an attempt to improve it.
note: Kay also writes of 'Simula leading to OOP' in the same paper.

label: learning by programming

audit_note: Version 3: quote replaced by one that states the influence.

label: simpler Smalltalk: prototypes, no classes
citation: Ungar, D. & Smith, R. B. (2007). Self. Proc. HOPL III (ACM SIGPLAN History of Programming Languages).

note: The paper also says confusion over Smalltalk-80's metaclasses 'gave us a strong push to eliminate classes when we designed Self'. The authors never call Self a Smalltalk 'dialect'.

label: syntax, minus pointers
citation: Gosling, J. & McGilton, H. (1996). The Java Language Environment: A White Paper. Sun Microsystems.
quote: keeping the Java programming language looking like C++ as far as possible results in it being a familiar language, while removing the unnecessary complexities of C++.
note: The same white paper says 'There are no explicit programmer-defined pointer data types, no pointer arithmetic' and, in section 2 (simple-familiar.html), 'Java has no pointer data types.'

label: object-oriented concepts (no feature given)

quote: Design and architecture decisions drew from a variety of languages such as Eiffel, SmallTalk, Objective C, and Cedar/Mesa.
note: Label revised to match the source. The white paper credits Smalltalk only in general terms and does not link it to the VM or GC. In 'A Conversation with James Gosling' (ACM Queue, 2004, https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=1017013) Gosling says a p-code translator 'formed the core of the design' and that he then consulted 'people like Peter Deutsch who had worked on the Smalltalk VMs'.

citation: Morris, R. (2009). Anders Hejlsberg: Geek of the Week (interview). Simple Talk, Redgate.
quote: Java certainly demonstrated the value of type safety, exception handling, and garbage collection in a mainstream programming language. [...] Many programming languages influenced C#. Java was one of them, but C++ and Delphi also influenced our design.
note: Label revised to match the source. Hejlsberg confirms the Java influence and names type safety, exceptions and GC (the interviewer calls Java a 'managed platform'). He does not mention classes or interfaces.

label: C-family syntax
citation: Morris, R. (2009). Anders Hejlsberg: Geek of the Week (interview). Simple Talk, Redgate.
quote: Many programming languages influenced C#. Java was one of them, but C++ and Delphi also influenced our design.
note: Label revised to match the source. Microsoft's C# overview (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/tour-of-csharp/overview) says 'C# is in the C family of languages' and that its syntax is familiar to C/C++ users. No source found that credits operator overloading to C++.

label: properties, events, is/as (same designer, Hejlsberg)

citation: Morris, R. (2009). Anders Hejlsberg: Geek of the Week (interview). Simple Talk, Redgate.

note: Label made specific; the features are widely described but not stated in the cited source. Label limited to the documented claim: Hejlsberg names Delphi as an influence and lists properties and events among C#'s differences from Java, without attributing them to Delphi. The Artima interview 'Delegates, Components, and Simplexity' (2003) discusses first-class properties and events but does not mention Delphi. Drawn dotted because the source gives no strength.

label: classes, JVM interop
citation: Odersky, M. (2006). A Brief History of Scala. Artima Weblogs.
quote: Scala is not an extension of Java, but it is completely interoperable with it. Scala translates to Java bytecodes, and the efficiency of its compiled programs usually equals Java's.
note: Odersky et al., 'An Overview of the Scala Programming Language' (2006) adds that 'Scala adopts a large part of the concepts and syntactic conventions of Java and C#.'
audit_note: Version 3: kind design to syntax.

label: abstract types, after ML's module systems
citation: Odersky, M. et al. (2006). An Overview of the Scala Programming Language, Second Edition. EPFL Technical Report LAMP-REPORT-2006-001, section 10 (Related Work).
quote: Scala's abstract types have close resemblances to abstract types of signatures in the module systems of ML [24] and OCaml [29], generalizing them to a context of first-class components.
audit_note: Version 3: strength strong to weak; kind design to type; verdict supported to partly; quote and source updated; label revised.

label: type classes
citation: Odersky, M., Spoon, L. & Venners, B. (2008). Programming in Scala, 1st ed., ch. 1 'Scala's roots'. Artima.
quote: Scala's implicit parameters were motivated by Haskell's type classes; they achieve analogous results in a more classical object-oriented setting.
note: Also in Odersky et al., 'An Overview of the Scala Programming Language' (2006): 'Views have been influenced by Haskell's type classes.'

quote: The most widely taught language is now (or will be soon, in any case) Python, which is indentation based.
note: Python is one of several precedents in Odersky's rationale, alongside Haskell, F#, Elm, Agda, Idris, Markdown and YAML. He cites it to show the style is familiar, not as a direct model. The Scala 3 reference page on optional braces names no other language.

label: pipelines, but of objects
citation: Snover, J. (2002). Monad Manifesto. Microsoft (republished at jsnover.com).
quote: Unlike cmd.exe, the Monad shell is based upon and extends the Bourne Shell syntax and control structures facilitating the skill transfer of Unix Admins.
note: The manifesto also says MSH uses 'the functions and syntax of the POSIX Shell model ... as a starting point' and criticizes the text-based UNIX pipeline.
audit_note: Version 3: quote replaced by one that states the influence.

label: C#-like syntax (glide path to C#)
citation: Snover, J. (2002). Monad Manifesto. Microsoft (republished at jsnover.com).
quote: These are then modified and expanded upon to either improve the programming experience, take advantage of new functionality or provide a glide path to C#.
note: Label revised to match the source. 'These' are the POSIX-shell-based script constructs. Cmdlets are written 'in C#, VB.NET, COBOL, etc'. The .NET objects come from the CLR platform, not from C#, so the C# link is the cmdlet language and a deliberate syntactic glide path.

label: let/where, expression language
citation: MacQueen, D., Harper, R. & Reppy, J. (2020). The History of Standard ML. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 86.
quote: The basic framework of the language design was inspired by Peter Landin's ISWIM language from the mid 1960s [1966b], which was, in turn, a sugared syntax for Church's lambda calculus.
note: The same paper describes ISWIM as an applied call-by-value lambda calculus 'with syntactic sugar (e.g., "where" and "let" declaration constructs)', and says ML followed ISWIM in strict evaluation and allowing impure features.

label: ISWIM's applicative core, via PAL, SASL and KRC
citation: Turner, D. A. (2012). Some History of Functional Programming Languages. Invited lecture, Trends in Functional Programming (TFP 2012), St Andrews.
quote: ISWIM inspired PAL (Evans 1968) at MIT / a simple DL based on the applicative subset of PAL / Miranda is essentially SASL plus algebraic types and the polymorphic type discipline of Milner (1978).
note: Turner's chain is ISWIM, then PAL, then SASL, then KRC ('a miniaturized version of SASL', where guards first appeared), then Miranda. He also credits ISWIM directly for having no explicit lambdas and for the offside rule.

label: Hindley-Milner types
citation: Hudak, P., Hughes, J., Peyton Jones, S. & Wadler, P. (2007). A History of Haskell: Being Lazy with Class. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: Type classes provided a uniform solution to both of these problems. They generalised the notion of equality type variables from SML, introducing a notion of a “class” of types that possessed a given set of operations (such as numeric operations or equality).
note: The paper also says Miranda already had a Hindley-Milner type system, so this influence also reached Haskell through Miranda. Type classes generalized SML's equality type variables.
audit_note: Version 3: quote replaced by one that states the influence.

label: lazy, pure (open rewrite)
citation: Hudak, P., Hughes, J., Peyton Jones, S. & Wadler, P. (2007). A History of Haskell: Being Lazy with Class. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: Haskell’s design was, therefore, strongly influenced by Miranda. At the time, Miranda was the fullest expression of a non-strict, purely functional language with a Hindley-Milner type system and algebraic data types—and that was precisely the kind of language that Haskell aspired to be.
note: The committee asked Turner whether Miranda could be the starting point, and he declined. Miranda's license required permission before distributing an implementation or a substantially copied language, and a freely available language was one of Haskell's stated goals.
audit_note: Version 3: quote replaced by one that states the influence.

label: dialect + objects
citation: OCaml.org (n.d.). About OCaml / history. Official OCaml website.
quote: It was inspired by a long line of research into ML / The modern OCaml emerged in 1996, when Didier Rémy and Jérôme Vouillon implemented a powerful and elegant object system.
note: This is the official site rather than a paper. It traces ML to LCF and Caml to INRIA in 1987. Note that it dates LCF/ML to 1972, while other sources say 1973.

label: OCaml for .NET
citation: Syme, D. (2020). The Early History of F#. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 75.
quote: The early conception of F# was simple: to bring the benefits of OCaml to .NET and .NET to OCaml
note: The working name was 'Caml.NET', and the 2002 announcement called F# 'an implementation of the core of the Caml programming language for the .NET Framework'. Syme notes it was never fully compatible with any OCaml version.

label: pipe operator |>
citation: Valim, J. (2018). Post in 'Which language first introduced the pipe operator?'. Elixir Forum.
quote: Almost sure we got it from F# but somebody pointed early on that it existed in ML before that.
note: The |> operator itself dates from Isabelle/ML (1994).

label: functional; 'similar to F#' (Microsoft)
citation: Microsoft (n.d.). Power Query M formula language. Microsoft Learn.
quote: The M language is a functional, case-sensitive language similar to F#.
note: Microsoft states a similarity, not an influence. The M spec introduction (m-spec-introduction) calls M 'mostly pure, higher-order, dynamically typed, partially lazy', models its evaluation on spreadsheets, and does not mention F#.

label: pipe |>, via magrittr; native in R 4.1
citation: Bache, S. M. & Wickham, H. (n.d.). Introducing magrittr (package vignette), CRAN; and Tierney, L. (n.d.). Native pipe design note (PIPE.md), R Project SVN.
quote: a prime example is the |> operator used extensively in F# (to say the least) and indeed this – along with Unix pipes – served as a motivation for developing the magrittr package.
note: Influence by the library route. Library link: R core's design note for the native pipe (R 4.1) cites magrittr, not F#.

label: LAMBDA (MSR functional-programming research)
citation: Microsoft Research Podcast (2021). Advancing Excel as a programming language with Andy Gordon and Simon Peyton Jones.
quote: the North Star of mainstream functional programming languages
note: Later feature: LAMBDA (2020) came from Microsoft Research's functional-programming work with Haskell co-designer Simon Peyton Jones; Haskell itself is not named as the source.

label: Bourne Again
citation: Ramey, C. & Fox, B. (current ed.). Bash Reference Manual, §1.1 "What is Bash?". Free Software Foundation (copy hosted by Chet Ramey, Case Western Reserve University).
quote: The name is an acronym for the 'Bourne-Again SHell', a pun on Stephen Bourne, the author of the direct ancestor of the current Unix shell sh
note: Same section: 'Bash is largely compatible with sh and incorporates useful features from the Korn shell ksh and the C shell csh.' gnu.org refused automated fetching, so the maintainer's mirror was used.

label: shell features (Wall names sh)
citation: Wall, L. (1987). perl(1) manual page, Perl 1.0 (header dated 87/12/18). Distributed with Perl 1.0 (2.11BSD source archive).
quote: It combines (in the author's opinion, anyway) some of the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh, so people familiar with those languages should have little difficulty with it.
note: In 1987 'sh' meant the Bourne shell; the same page adds 'Language historians will also note some vestiges of csh, Pascal, and even BASIC-PLUS.' The current perl(1) at perldoc.perl.org says 'sed, awk, and sh' and drops C.

label: awk-style text scanning, reports
citation: Wall, L. (1987). perl(1) manual page, Perl 1.0 (header dated 87/12/18). Distributed with Perl 1.0 (2.11BSD source archive).
quote: It combines (in the author's opinion, anyway) some of the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh, so people familiar with those languages should have little difficulty with it.
note: Same DESCRIPTION: Perl 'combines ... some of the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh' and 'There are also translators to turn your sed and awk scripts into perl scripts.' The page names awk as a source but does not single out its patterns; the regex side is equally credited to sed.
audit_note: Version 3: quote replaced by one that states the influence.

note: The same page lists C first among 'the best features of C, sed, awk, and sh'.
audit_note: Version 3: quote replaced by one that states the influence.

quote: Flow of control within an awk action can be achieved using the statements if-else, while, for, and statement grouping with braces, as in C.
note: The paper also says 'the C increment ++ and decrement -- operators are also available' and that printf matches 'the standard I/O library used with the programming language C'. Venue taken from the file name and standard bibliographies; the PDF's first page shows only Bell Laboratories.

citation: Griswold, R. E. (1994). Icon in the Humanities. TEXT Technology 4(1), 13-19 (online version updated 1996, University of Arizona).

note: Griswold also calls Icon 'in some ways, a successor to SNOBOL4' and says string scanning answered weaknesses in SNOBOL4's pattern matching. The Icon Version 5 Reference Manual (Griswold et al., 1981; https://gmorph.cs.arizona.edu/icon/ftp/doc/tr81_4a.pdf) says SNOBOL4-style patterns 'were replaced by the concept of string scanning'. String scanning is Icon's replacement for SNOBOL4 patterns, not something taken from SNOBOL.

note: Guido credits his DEC SRC exposure to Modula-2+ and Modula-3. For classes, the Python Tutorial §9 says the class mechanism 'is a mixture of the class mechanisms found in C++ and Modula-3'.
